Medical Neuroanatomy · Chapter 3 · Case 3-2

Penetrating Stab Wound to the Back — Right Hemicord Injury

27-year-old man, knife wound entering the spinal column at the scapular level — worked up for a Brown-Séquard–pattern cord injury.

Text 100%
Localization Finding Term Pattern Workup / Trajectory

Chief Complaint

A 27-year-old right-handed machinist was brought by ambulance to the emergency room after suffering a knife wound in the back. He was conscious but somewhat intoxicated1. A penetrating wound2 was present on his back, slightly off the midline and opposite the superior border of the right scapula3.

History of Chief Complaint

He had been involved in an altercation in a local tavern. The knife wound was received at 1:35am4, after an evening spent watching a national sports event and consuming alcoholic beverages.

Family History

He is single and lives in an apartment. He has two brothers and a sister. His mother and father are divorced.5

Physical Examination

This is a stable male patient with a penetrating wound on his right back that entered the spinal column6. It is located on the right and approximately one inch above and medial to the spine of the scapula. The patient is an awake, intoxicated male. He is large, muscular, well nourished, well hydrated7, and appears his stated age. Blood pressure, heart rate, and respirations were slightly elevated8; peripheral pulses were intact at the wrists and ankles9.

Neurologic Examination

Mental Status

He was awake but somewhat intoxicated. Affect is agitated and bellicose10; problems with cooperation occurred. Speech was slurred and rambling; however, no word substitution or word confusion was present11. Memory and knowledge could not be tested adequately because of his level of intoxication.

Cranial Nerves

A full range of eye movements was present. Visual fields were full to confrontation12. Hearing was normal bilaterally. Pupillary, gag, and corneal reflexes were intact13; facial movements were full; uvula and tongue were midline.

Motor Systems

There is a proximal-to-distal, graded diminution of strength in the upper extremity on the right14. Power was 4/5 for shoulder elevation, 3/5 for the forearm flexors and extensors, 1/5 for the flexors and extensors of the wrist and in the fingers. Grip strength was abolished completely15. All strength was absent in the right lower extremity16. Deep tendon reflexes were depressed about the elbow (1/4) and absent about the wrist and in the digits as well as throughout the lower extremity (0/4)17. Clonus could be obtained on forceful dorsiflexion of the right ankle18.

Sensory Systems

Complete loss of sensation for pinprick and temperature was found over the left trunk below C8 and in the left lower extremity19. Loss of discriminative touch and vibratory sense was found over the right half of the body below and including C820.

Follow-up

Two weeks later21 a neurologic examination revealed no change in the distribution of sensory loss22. Strength remained diminished in the forearm, hand, and complete lower extremity on the right, and deep tendon reflexes around the right elbow remained diminished at 1/4. However, the following changes had occurred: deep tendon reflexes were elevated at the wrist, finger, knee, and ankle on the right side (approximately 3/4)23. A positive Babinski sign could be elicited from the right foot24.

Questions

  1. Has the patient experienced any changes in consciousness or cognition, language function or spatial recognition, personality or emotional behavior, or any loss in memory?
  2. Does the patient exhibit any loss of vision and if so, where in the visual field is the loss? Are there any visual hallucinations present in this patient?
  3. Are there any changes in cranial nerve function and if so, are they signs of suprasegmental or segmental level defects?

Clinical Reasoning Walkthrough

From wound to diagnosis

01 · Localization

Right hemicord, ~C8

The stab wound entered the spinal column near the scapular spine, but cord segments sit higher than their matching vertebral level in this region — placing the lesion around C8. The exam is a textbook hemicord pattern: ipsilateral (right) corticospinal and dorsal-column loss, with contralateral (left) spinothalamic loss below the level.

02 · Distribution

Focal, unilateral, tract-selective

This is a discrete structural injury to one side of the cord, not a diffuse or length-dependent process. The dissociated sensory pattern (different tracts, different sides) only makes sense as damage to a specific hemicord cross-section.

03 · Time Course

Acute, evolving over two weeks

Deficits appeared immediately with the stab wound (acute onset). The two-week follow-up shows the expected evolution out of spinal shock: reflexes below the lesion flip from depressed/absent to hyperreflexic, and a Babinski sign appears — unmasking the true upper motor neuron character of the injury.

04 · Differential Diagnosis

DiagnosisFitsArgues against
Brown-Séquard syndrome (hemicord)Most likely Penetrating trauma at the right cord level; ipsilateral motor + dorsal-column loss; contralateral pain/temp loss; late hyperreflexia and Babinski —
Complete cord transection Trauma, severe deficit Deficits are not uniform bilaterally — there's a clear side-to-side dissociation
Anterior cord syndrome Motor and pain/temp loss present Dorsal columns are affected here (ipsilaterally); anterior cord syndrome classically spares them
Central cord syndrome Cervical-level trauma Would expect a cape-like, arm-predominant pattern, not this crossed dissociation with complete leg involvement
Peripheral nerve / brachial plexus injury Proximal-to-distal arm weakness gradient could superficially suggest this Doesn't explain contralateral leg sensory loss or the later corticospinal (UMN) signs

05 · Diagnostic Workup

  1. Spine CTCharacterize the bony injury and locate any retained blade fragment or foreign material along the wound tract.
  2. MRI spineOnce stable — define cord edema, hematoma, and the anatomic extent of the hemicord lesion.
  3. Chest imagingThe wound sits near the lung apex and pleura — rule out pneumothorax or hemothorax regardless of the neuro picture.
  4. Neurosurgical consultFor possible exploration or decompression if imaging shows a compressive hematoma or retained foreign body.

06 · Prognosis

Of the incomplete cord injury syndromes, Brown-Séquard generally carries the best outlook for functional recovery — substantial improvement in strength is common over time. Ipsilateral proprioceptive/vibratory loss and contralateral pain/temperature loss, however, can be more persistent than the motor deficit.

07 · Management

  • Spinal stabilization and surgical wound exploration
  • Physical/occupational therapy for the evolving weakness
  • Bladder and bowel function monitoring
  • Autonomic function (bladder, bowel, sexual) is usually preserved in a true hemicord injury, since these pathways have bilateral innervation — bilateral autonomic deficits would point toward a different or more extensive process
  • Spasticity and neuropathic pain management as UMN signs progress
  • Surgical decompression if imaging shows ongoing cord compression

Concept Deep-Dive

The neuroanatomy behind the exam

click any image to enlarge

Localization

Right hemicord at a glance

The concept in one picture — half the cord is out.

AMBOSS — Brown-Séquard syndrome. This example marks the lesion at T8; our patient's is around C8, but the logic is identical at any level.

  • Lateral corticospinal tract (already crossed above) → weakness on the same side as the lesion, below it.
  • Dorsal columns (not yet crossed) → loss of vibration/proprioception on the same side as the lesion, below it.
  • Spinothalamic tract (already crossed a segment or two below where it entered) → pain/temperature loss on the opposite side.

As one small-group framed it: the patient effectively lost an entire half of the cord's cross-section at that level — sensory information above the injury can't get up to the brain, and motor commands can't get down past it, but only on that one side.

Localization

Orientation: the full tract map, then zoom in

Every named ascending (sensory, blue) and descending (motor, red) tract, with somatotopic layering (C = cervical, T = thoracic, L = lumbar, S = sacral).

The two tracts that actually matter for this case, boxed for emphasis.

There's a lot on that first map, but only three systems are doing any work in this case: the dorsal columns (fine touch, vibration, proprioception), the lateral spinothalamic tract (pain, temperature, crude touch), and the lateral corticospinal tract (voluntary movement). Everything else — spinocerebellar tracts, the spino-olivary tract, and the extrapyramidal tracts (reticulospinal, rubrospinal, vestibulospinal, olivospinal, tectospinal) — is along for the ride but isn't what the exam findings are testing here.

Knowing the whole map matters for boards, but knowing which three tracts are "live wires" in a given case is what actually gets you to the diagnosis fastest.

Localization

Dorsal column–medial lemniscus: the “onion” pathway

Dorsal column system (left) vs. spinothalamic tract (right) — same three-neuron structure, very different crossing point.

Whiteboard version, drawn the way it was worked through in small group.

Think of each fasciculus (gracilis, then cuneatus) like an onion built from the inside out. Fibers carrying touch/vibration/proprioception from the sacral cord join closest to the midline; as you go up the cord, each new spinal level's fibers get added to the outside of that bundle rather than pushed toward the center — so by the time you reach the neck, cervical fibers sit most lateral and sacral fibers sit most medial.

The whole bundle stays on the same side all the way up to the medulla. Only there does it synapse (nucleus gracilis/cuneatus) and cross the midline — via the internal arcuate fibers — to join the medial lemniscus on the opposite side. Because the crossing happens that high up, a spinal cord lesion below it produces ipsilateral loss of vibration, proprioception, and fine touch.

This patient's dorsal column loss is on the right — the same side as his wound — because at C8 these fibers haven't crossed yet and won't for many segments.

The bedside test for this pathway: remove vision (eyes closed) and a dorsal-column deficit unmasks itself as swaying — a positive Romberg sign.

Localization

Anterolateral system: why C8 itself wasn't included

Notice the anterior white commissure crossing point is drawn separately at the cervical and lumbar levels — the crossing is local to each level, not instantaneous.

The anterolateral funiculus (spinothalamic tract) sits opposite the posterior/dorsal funiculus — already-crossed fibers, on the wound side.

Spinothalamic fibers synapse in the dorsal horn and cross almost immediately — but "almost" is the key word. They angle across through the anterior white commissure over a level or two before fully joining the tract on the opposite side, instead of crossing instantly at the exact segment they entered.

That short lag creates a “fuzzy zone” a segment or two tall, right at the level of injury, where the crossing is incomplete. A lesion there won't cleanly knock out that exact segment on the opposite side — the deficit shows up starting just below it instead.

For reference: order-of-neurons across the major sensory pathways.

That's exactly this patient's pattern: his dorsal column (uncrossed) loss includes C8, but his contralateral pain/temperature loss starts below C8 — C8 itself was still mid-crossing when the wound hit.

Localization

Dermatomes: what “C8” actually looks like on skin

C8 runs down the ulnar side of the arm into the ring and little fingers — that's the strip a "C8 sensory level" actually refers to.

A "level" on paper is one thing; a dermatome map is what turns it into something you can actually check at the bedside. C8 covers the medial forearm and the ulnar one-and-a-half fingers — nowhere near the thumb (that's C6) or the palm's radial side (C7). When the case says "loss below C8," this map is what tells you exactly where to run the pin.

This is also why the exact vertebral-level-vs-cord-segment offset matters so much in this case (see the wound-level annotation above): get the segment wrong by even one level and you're testing the wrong strip of skin entirely.

Localization

Corticospinal somatotopy: why the leg was hit harder

Cross-section somatotopy: leg fibers sit most superficial/lateral in both the dorsal columns and the lateral corticospinal tract.

The corticospinal tract already crosses at the decussation of the pyramids in the medulla — long before it reaches C8. Orange = upper motor neuron, teal = lower motor neuron.

Inside the lateral corticospinal tract, fibers are stacked somatotopically: cervical (arm) fibers sit deep and medial, sacral (leg) fibers sit superficial and lateral. A blade entering from the back reaches the superficial fibers first and hardest.

That's why this patient's leg was knocked out completely while his arm showed a graded, only partial weakness — the injury simply didn't reach the deeper cervical fibers as fully.

Workup / Trajectory

Spinal shock → the true UMN pattern unmasked

UMN signs (top) vs. LMN signs (bottom) — this patient shows both, at different times.

The basic reflex arc a DTR is testing: stretch receptor → one synapse in the cord → contraction. No brain involved — which is exactly why the arc itself can stay intact even when everything above it goes quiet.

Normally, descending tracts keep a constant background “tone” on the reflex circuits below them. When the cord is suddenly cut off from that input, those circuits go quiet for a while — reflexes disappear and muscles go flaccid, even though the actual lesion (corticospinal tract damage) is an upper motor neuron problem. That temporary quiet period is spinal shock, and it's exactly why this patient's day-one exam reads as diminished/absent reflexes despite what will turn out to be a UMN-type lesion.

Clonus at the ankle on day one is the tell that the reflex arc and the lower motor neurons themselves are still intact — they're just running unopposed. Over the next one to two weeks those circuits regain their own excitability, and the reflexes swing the other way: hyperreflexia, spasticity, and a Babinski sign appear, revealing the upper motor neuron lesion that was there all along.

This patient's elbow reflex (above the lesion) stayed flat at 1/4 both times, while everything below it flipped from areflexic to hyperreflexic with a new Babinski — a clean before/after of spinal shock resolving.

Localization

Segmental vs. suprasegmental

Cortical / brainstem signs present?
NO ↓YES ↓
Segmental
(spinal cord) — this patient
Suprasegmental
(brain)

eye movements full · visual fields full · no aphasia · CN reflexes intact

  • No aphasia, no visual field cut, full eye movements, intact cranial nerve reflexes — none of these support a brain-level lesion.
  • Altered mentation here is explained by intoxication, not by a cortical process.

This is the direct answer to the case's own Questions 1–3: the deficits are segmental (spinal), not suprasegmental — the brain exam is normal.

Pattern

Spinal cord syndromes at a glance

Descending (motor, left half shown) vs. ascending (sensory, right half shown) tracts on one cross-section — Brown-Séquard is simply a lesion of everything on one side of that midline.

SyndromeMotorPain/tempVibration/proprio.
Brown-SéquardIpsilateral lossContralateral lossIpsilateral loss
Complete transectionBilateral lossBilateral lossBilateral loss
Anterior cordBilateral lossBilateral lossSpared
Central cordArms > legsCape-like, variableOften spared

Only the Brown-Séquard row produces a different side for motor/vibration versus pain/temperature — the exact dissociation documented in this patient's sensory exam.

Workup / Trajectory

Blood supply of the cord: thirds, not halves

Anterior spinal artery (midline, anterior) vs. paired posterior spinal arteries.

Edited pathway table highlighting the dorsal-column relay: dorsal root ganglion to gracile and cuneate nuclei, then to the contralateral VPL of the thalamus.

A knife makes a clean left/right split. Blood supply doesn't work that way — it's organized front-to-back, not side-to-side. A single anterior spinal artery supplies the anterior two-thirds of the cord (both corticospinal tracts, both spinothalamic tracts, both anterior horns), while a pair of posterior spinal arteries each cover one dorsal column.

That's why a vascular insult like anterior spinal artery occlusion produces bilateral weakness and bilateral pain/temperature loss with the dorsal columns spared — a completely different pattern from this patient's clean, one-sided hemicord injury, and exactly why the differential table rules out anterior cord syndrome.

Workup / Trajectory

Further study: spinal cord pathways, start to finish

Good one to watch once the case makes sense on its own — it's the same three systems above (dorsal columns, spinothalamic, corticospinal) walked through end to end.
